links.note: Why the plough horse needed glasses - to keep the sun out of its eyes while ploughing. One of the animal patients arriving at Dolittle's practice, not the Cat's-meat-Man's suggestion (28259).
What the plough horse needed instead of pills - spectacles. An episode of Dolittle's animal practice rather than a point about his knowledge versus the vets' (28265).
Farm animals wearing glasses becoming a common sight around Puddleby - the practice growing, which is 28258's subject.
How animals communicate besides their mouths - with ears, feet, tails, everything. Polynesia's lesson is the basis of Dolittle knowing more about animals than the local vets.
What the twitching of the dog's nose meant - 'Can't you see that it has stopped raining?'. Animal language, the knowledge that sets Dolittle above the vets.
Polynesia explaining that animals talk with their ears, feet and tails and sometimes prefer not to make a noise - the animal-language knowledge in 28265.
What 'Ka-ka oi-ee, fee-fee?' means in bird language - 'Is the porridge hot yet?'. Bird language, so 28265 and not 28263, which is the learner's own choice of animal.
How the story shows the importance of understanding animals: learning their languages, diagnosing the horse's blindness where the vets could not. That is 28265's claim.
Suggest an alternative title for the poem - 'The Topsy-Turvy Man', for his upside-down actions. The poem's single comic figure and what he does.
Why the poet included dialogues in the poem - they make the exchange with the funny man lively. About the poem's comic figure, not the play's scenes (28273).
What the speaker said about the 'rose' after smelling the bun - 'a funny looking smell'. That phrase applies sight to smell, which is exactly the sense-crossing 28270 names.
How the poet's playful language works - 'funny sounding sight' and 'funny looking smell' whimsically mix the senses. 28270 lists those very phrases.
The overall tone of the poem - humorous and whimsical. The comedy the poem builds around the funny man.
How the poet reacted to the 'rose's' smell - she staggered back. Part of the exchange with the funny man.
How the poet reacts to the currant bun - staggering back and playing along with his joke. The funny man's antic and its effect.
What the repeated stage direction 'no one speaks' indicates. Stage directions are read only because the text is set out as a play, which is 28273.
What kind of story 'Say the Right Thing' is - a humorous play. Identifying the form, which 28273 covers: scenes with speakers named, read differently from prose or a poem.
Choosing which statements display polite behaviour when you have guests - accompanying them to the door. This is 28275's exercise verbatim.
The same polite-behaviour selection, continuing into three ways of handling classmates who are rude while disagreeing. Politeness judgement, not the play's plot.
What Mrs Harding's and Mrs Lee's restrained responses to Mary's blunders reveal - politeness and patience. Recognising polite behaviour in the guests.
Mary's final blunder, 'Oh, must you stay? Can't you go?' - the clearest instance of a statement that does not display polite behaviour.
Which quality Mary lacks with the guests - politeness. Named directly, so 28275.
The central theme of Mary's mistakes - the impact of words and the need for sensitive communication. A politeness judgement rather than Mrs Shaw's preparations (28272).
Mary's first blunder - complimenting Mrs Harding's children, who do not exist. An impolite remark, so 28275.
The profession Mary unintentionally insulted - bankers, Mrs Lee's brother's. Recognising the remark as impolite.
What Mary said about Mrs Cotter staying in bed and calling the doctor - an offensive remark, since Mrs Harding does the same.
Mary calling Mrs Grantley 'too talkative' and not interesting - another statement on the impolite side of 28275's sort.
The impact of Mary's continuous blunders - the guests felt embarrassed and uncomfortable. What impolite talk does, which is 28275.
Listening task item: the son behaved impatiently in the grocery queue. The whole listening passage sorts polite from impolite behaviour, which is 28275.
